t: eBPF: What eBPF Is: Safe Programs in the Kernel
title: eBPF: What eBPF Is: Safe Programs in the Kernel
description: eBPF lets you run sandboxed programs inside the Linux kernel without changing kernel source or loading risky modules. You write a small C (or higher-level) program, the kernel's verifier proves it cannot crash or hang the system, and it attaches to hooks: kprobes on kernel functions, tracepoints, XDP on the network driver, or TC on traffic control. The program can inspect packets, count syscalls, and share data with user space through maps. It is the technology behind Cilium networking, Falco runtime security, and modern observability — kernel superpowers with a safety proof.

t: eBPF: The Verifier: Why eBPF Cannot Crash the Kernel
title: eBPF: The Verifier: Why eBPF Cannot Crash the Kernel
description: The verifier is eBPF's safety core: before a program loads, the kernel statically analyzes every path — bounded loops only, no null dereferences, no out-of-bounds map access, no leaking kernel pointers. If the proof fails, the program is rejected with a diagnostic. This is what makes eBPF deployable where kernel modules are not: the safety argument is checked by the kernel itself, on every load. Understanding verifier errors (the famous 'unbounded loop' rejections) is the first eBPF debugging skill.
key_facts: Bounded loops, no bad memory access
Rejections logged with the violated rule

t: eBPF: Maps: How Kernel Programs Talk to User Space
title: eBPF: Maps: How Kernel Programs Talk to User Space
description: eBPF programs cannot print freely, so they communicate through maps — key/value stores shared between kernel and user space: hash maps for counters, ring buffers and perf buffers for event streams, LRU maps for connection tracking. A packet counter increments a map in XDP; a user-space daemon reads it once a second and graphs it. Designing the map layout is designing the telemetry: what you count in-kernel determines what you can ever know in user space.

t: eBPF: XDP: Filtering at the Driver, Before the Stack
title: eBPF: XDP: Filtering at the Driver, Before the Stack
description: XDP (eXpress Data Path) runs eBPF at the earliest possible point — in the network driver, before the kernel allocates a socket buffer. An XDP program can drop, pass, redirect, or modify packets at millions of packets per second per core, which is why it is the backbone of DDoS mitigation: attack traffic dies at the driver while legitimate traffic flows. Writing an XDP drop rule is a few dozen lines of C, and the performance is within reach of dedicated hardware.
key_facts: Earliest hook: inside the network driver

t: eBPF: Your First Trace: bpftrace One-Liners
title: eBPF: Your First Trace: bpftrace One-Liners
description: The hello-world of eBPF is bpftrace: 'bpftrace -e \'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat { printf("%s %s\\n", comm, str(args->filename)); }\'' prints every file opened on the system with the process name. One-liners like this replace hours of strace archaeology: count syscalls by process, histogram read latencies, watch TCP retransmits live. bpftrace compiles the one-liner to eBPF, the verifier approves it, and you get kernel-level truth in seconds.

console.log('peep: trace opens by process (role: net-auditor)');

t: eBPF: bcc: The Toolkit of Ready-Made Tracers
title: eBPF: bcc: The Toolkit of Ready-Made Tracers
description: bcc (BPF Compiler Collection) ships dozens of production tracers: opensnoop, execsnoop, tcpconnect, tcplife, biosnoop, runqlat — each a Python frontend over eBPF programs. They are the fastest path from 'something is wrong' to 'here is the evidence': which process opened which file, which connections lived how long, which disk I/O stalled. For incident response on a Linux fleet, bcc literacy is a superpower — it turns the kernel into a witness.

t: eBPF: CO-RE: Compile Once, Run Everywhere
title: eBPF: CO-RE: Compile Once, Run Everywhere
description: Kernel versions change struct layouts, which used to mean recompiling eBPF for every kernel. CO-RE (Compile Once, Run Everywhere) fixes this with BTF type information: the program records field offsets symbolically and the loader relocates them against the running kernel. One binary runs across the fleet's kernel versions. For heterogeneous defense fleets — and it is always heterogeneous — CO-RE is what makes eBPF operationally sane.
key_facts: BTF relocates struct offsets at load

t: eBPF: Defensive Uses: Runtime Security with Falco
title: eBPF: Defensive Uses: Runtime Security with Falco
description: eBPF's premier defensive application is runtime security: Falco watches syscalls with eBPF and alerts on suspicious behavior — a shell spawned in a container, sensitive files read at 3 AM, unexpected outbound connections. Because the sensor is in the kernel, user-space malware cannot blind it the way it can blind user-space agents. The rules are declarative YAML; the enforcement point is the kernel itself. This is defense that sees everything and can be evaded only with kernel exploits.

t: eBPF: Networking: Cilium and eBPF Service Mesh
title: eBPF: Networking: Cilium and eBPF Service Mesh
description: Cilium replaces kube-proxy iptables with eBPF: load balancing, network policy, and observability all run as verified programs in the kernel. The result is faster networking with per-packet policy enforcement and Hubble's flow-level visibility. For tactical Kubernetes at the edge, this matters twice: fewer moving parts to secure, and policy that is actually enforced at packet speed rather than documented in YAML and hoped for.

t: eBPF: Debugging: When the Verifier Says No
title: eBPF: Debugging: When the Verifier Says No
description: Every eBPF engineer meets the verifier's rejections: 'unbounded loop', 'invalid memory access', 'too many instructions'. The debugging ladder is: read the verifier log (it names the failing instruction), simplify the program until it loads, then re-add complexity piece by piece; use bpf_printk and the trace pipe for runtime printf; and keep programs small — split logic across tail calls or move aggregation to user space. The verifier is not your enemy; it is the reason your program is safe to run in production kernels.

title: eBPF: Performance: Profiling with eBPF
description: eBPF is also a profiler: stack-trace sampling at configurable rates builds flame graphs of where CPU actually goes, with negligible overhead. Off-CPU analysis shows where threads block — the I/O and lock waits that on-CPU profilers miss. For latency-sensitive defense systems, this is how you find the 2 ms nobody can explain: sample the kernel's truth instead of guessing from application logs.

t: eBPF: LSM + eBPF: Programmable Access Control
title: eBPF: LSM + eBPF: Programmable Access Control
description: eBPF programs can attach to the Linux Security Module hooks, making access-control decisions in verified code: allow or deny file opens, socket creates, and process executions by policy. This turns the kernel's authorization points into programmable policy engines — mandatory access control written as eBPF instead of static SELinux rules. The defensive power is precision: policy can consider process lineage, time, and system state, not just labels.

t: eBPF: Testing: Verifier Suites and Selftests
title: eBPF: Testing: Verifier Suites and Selftests
description: eBPF's safety claims rest on testing: the kernel's selftests load thousands of programs — valid ones must load, invalid ones must be rejected — on every change to the verifier. Production users add their own layer: load every tap in a test kernel, fuzz the maps, and verify the user-space decoder against known event streams. A tap that passes selftests on the exact fleet kernels is a tap you can trust at 3 AM.

t: eBPF: Real-World Pattern: Fleet Intrusion Sensor
title: eBPF: Real-World Pattern: Fleet Intrusion Sensor
description: A complete pattern: every host in the fleet runs a signed tap-set — execsnoop-class process tracking, Falco-class syscall rules, and XDP rate guards — exporting to a local aggregator over the management network. The SOC sees one timeline per host with kernel-level fidelity; user-space compromise cannot silence the sensors. Rule updates are signed bundles rolled like config. When an incident hits, the kernel has already recorded the evidence.

t: eBPF: Mastery: The Kernel Introspection Playbook
title: eBPF: Mastery: The Kernel Introspection Playbook
description: eBPF mastery is a rare combination: C fluency, kernel internals, verifier empathy, and user-space data engineering for the telemetry firehose. The advanced moves are custom tracers for proprietary drivers, CO-RE libraries for fleet tools, and LSM policy engines. The mindset: the kernel is not a black box — it is an instrument, and eBPF is how you play it without breaking it.
